ISSUE
Adopt Resolution No. CC 2020-121, a resolution of the City Council of the City of
Palmdale, reciting the fact of the General Municipal Election held on November 3, 2020,
declaring the result and such matters as provided by law.

RECOMMENDATION
Adopt Resolution No. CC 2020-121, a resolution of the City Council of the City of
Palmdale, reciting the fact of the General Municipal Election held on November 3, 2020,
declaring the result and such matters as provided by law.

BACKGROUND
Resolution No. CC 2020-121 recites the fact of the General Municipal Election held on
November 3, 2020 for the purpose of electing a Mayor for the full term of two (2) years on
a citywide basis, the election of two Councilmembers elected by geographic Districts 1
and 2 for four (4) year terms, as well as a measure to increase the sales tax in the City of
Palmdale to ensure long-term fiscal sustainability.

DISCUSSION
The California Elections Code states that the governing body of the City shall meet to
approve the canvass of the election and install the newly elected officers. The City Clerk
shall enter on the records of the City Council, a statement of the results of the election.
Attached as (“Exhibit A”) is the Certificate of the Canvass of the Election Returns
provided by the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk, which declares
the results of the election.

  CITY OF PALMDALE, CALIFORNIA
  RESOLUTION NO. CC 2020-121

  A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF
  PALMDALE CALIFORNIA, RECITING THE FACT OF
  THE GENERAL MUNICIPAL ELECTION HELD ON
  NOVEMBER 3, 2020, DECLARING THE RESULT AND
  SUCH OTHER MATTERS AS PROVIDED BY LAW

  WHEREAS, a General Municipal Election was held and conducted in the City of
Palmdale, California, on Tuesday, November 3, 2020, as required by law; and

  WHEREAS, notice of the election was given in time, form and manner as
provided by law; that voting precincts and vote by mail ballet drop-off boxes were
properly established; that election officers were appointed and that in all respects the
election was held and conducted and the votes were cast, received and canvassed
and the returns made and declared in time, form and manner as required by the
provisions of the Election Code of the State of California for the holding of elections in
charter cities; and
  WHEREAS, pursuant to Resolution No. CC 2020-080, adopted by Council on
June 16, 2020, the County Election Department canvassed the returns of the election
and certified the results, the results were received and are attached and made a part
hereof as Exhibit “A”.

NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF
PALMDALE DOES HEREBY FIND, DETERMINE, RESOLVE AND ORDER AS
FOLLOWS:

  SECTION 1. That the whole number of ballots cast in the precincts except vote
by mail voter ballots and provisional ballots was 23,458.

  That the whole number of votes by mail voter and provisional ballots cast in the
City was 74,317, making a total of 97,775 ballots cast in the City.

  SECTION 2. That the names of the persons voted for at the election for Mayor
for a full term of two years are as follows:

ISSUE
Receive and file the monthly investment activity reports for October 2020.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council receive and file the monthly investment activity
reports for City of Palmdale and Successor Agency for October 2020.

BACKGROUND
Pursuant to Section 16 of the City of Palmdale and Successor Agency Investment
Policy, the City Treasurer shall prepare and present monthly and quarterly reports on
investments to the City Manager/Executive Director and the City Council/Directors. The
reports shall detail the type of investment, name of the issuer, purchase date, date of
maturity, amount of deposit, and rate of interest. This information shall be provided for
all City and Successor Agency pooled investments, as well as for Certificates of
Participation, Revenue Bonds, Tax Allocation Bonds, Assessment Districts and
Community Facilities District accounts which are managed by outside Fiscal Agents.

The monthly and quarterly reports provide a synopsis of the investment activity for the
City of Palmdale and Successor Agency. The reports provide information on assets,
allocations, average maturities, yields, and book valuations.

The interest rates presented are the most current rates available as of the date of this
report.
The market values presented for pooled City and Successor Agency investments are
based on closing prices for the related investment as of the date of this report. This
information was obtained from the Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg Financial Markets,
Capital Market Finances, or other reliable source of market prices.

DISCUSSION
Compliance with Investment Policy

For October, the invested portfolio amount for the City of Palmdale totaled
$184,717,431, a decrease of $4,845,004 from the previous month and $10,063,987
increase in comparison to last year. The decrease in overall portfolio balance from the
previous month is a result more cash disbursements during the month. Debt service
payments are the largest contributing factor for cash disbursements.

The par value of Successor Agency’s portfolio as of October, was $5,473,517. The
balance increased by $14,173 from last month due to quarterly interest earnings.

All investments meet criteria appropriate to Section 8 of the Investment Policy. The
portfolios are based on a combination of various investments, including CDs,
Corporate Notes, U.S. Treasury Securities and Government Agency Paper, each
adhering to portfolio percentage limitations.

The Finance Division is the custodian for the City and Successor Agency’s investment
portfolio and follows the three main principles of both entity’s investment policy to 1.)
Investment in financial instruments that mitigate the risk of monetary losses stemming
from market fluctuations, 2.) Establish and maintain a portfolio that has sufficient
liquidity to allow the City and Successor Agency to meet all anticipated cash
requirements, and 3.) Seek out investment instruments that provide a competitive
market rate of return.

Liquidity

One core approach the Finance Division focuses on, is providing liquidity to measure
up to the City and Successor Agency’s operational requirements. Thus, the Finance
Department is currently investing in two pooled funds, LAIF and CAMP. These are
intended for the daily operational activities, used for economic uncertainties and
maintenance needs. The pooled funds provide a higher liquidity ratio to ensure the
City and Successor Agency meet cash flow requirements.

Total LAIF balance for the City of Palmdale is $88,706,962 compared to $88,546,237
at the end of September.

Successor Agency LAIF balance at the end of October was $5,473,517, a 25.6
percent decrease from June. The decrease in balance is due to withdraws to cover
monthly expenses.

CAMP’s balance for City of Palmdale is $10,244,141, compared to September’s
balance of $10,242,499. Increase in balance is due to the reinvestment of monthly

   City Council Staff Report
DATE:  DECEMBER 15, 2020
TO:  HONORABLE MAYOR AND CITY COUNCIL
FROM:  CITY MANAGER’S OFFICE
  FINANCE DIVISION
DISTRICT:  All
SUBJECT:  APPROVE AGREEMENT A-7263 WITH JONES WALBAUM
  CORPORATION DBA AMERICAN BUSINESS MACHINES TO
  PROVIDE MAINTENANCE, RELATED SUPPLIES AND PAPER, AND
  MANAGED PRINT SERVICES IN THE AMOUNT OF $300,000.

ISSUE
Approve Agreement A-7263 Jones Walbaum Corporation dba American Business
Machines to provide maintenance, related supplies and paper, and managed print
services in the amount of $300,000.

RECOMMENDATION
It is recommended that the City Council:
  1. Approve Agreement A-7263 with Jones Walbaum Corporation dba American
  Business Machines for maintenance and managed print services, and related
  supplies and paper, in an amount of $300,000; and,
  2. Authorize the City Manager or his designee and City Attorney to negotiate the final
  terms of agreements and authorize the City Manager to execute the agreements.

BACKGROUND
On December 2, 2015, City Council approved Request for Proposal No. 15-001-1800
and awarded agreement A-5308 with Canon Financial Services, Inc. to provide leased
copiers. The City Council also awarded agreement A-5319 with Jones Walbaum
Corporation dba American Business Machines to provide maintenance, related supplies
and paper, and managed print services. Both agreements A-5308 and A-5319 are set
to expire on December 31, 2020.

On August 4, 2020, the City Council approved agreement A-7104 with Canon Financial
Services to provide leased copiers citywide. Agreement A-7263 with Jones Walbaum
Corporation dba American Business Machines an authorized Canon dealer, will provide
maintenance, related supplies and paper, and provide managed print services for all
Canon leased copiers citywide. The American Business Machines has the largest copier

service operation in the Antelope Valley, while providing services to multiple School
Districts and the City of Lancaster.

DISCUSSION
As a result of the COVID-19 pandemic that has caused the City revenue loss and
increased PPE related expenditures, the most economical route for the City is to enter
into a lease with Canon Financial Services and have services provided by American
Business Machines via the NASPO cooperative agreement No. 140595, in compliance
with PMC 3.08.090. The proposed 69-month agreement A-7263 would be set to expire in
December 2026 along with agreement A-7104. Some of the benefits American Business
Machines shall provide are the following:
    A full-time in-house staff support person for the City’s copy center Monday
  through Thursday 7:30am to 6:00pm.
    Will provide a dedicated service technician through their local Palmdale office.
    Under the maintenance agreement, they shall provide full comprehensive
  coverage for all replacement toners, drums, all parts, labor, service, and
  inspections.
    Will provide reasonable cost for all related supplies and paper, while including
  direct location delivery service at all Canon copier locations citywide.
    Will provided City staff monthly reports detailing all services calls.

FISCAL IMPACT
The cost to provide maintenance and managed print services and related supplies and
paper for the 69-month term is estimated at $300,000 budgeted in account 10118002-
722450.

STRATEGIC PLAN
Goal II: Ensure long-term fiscal health of the City and maintain funding for services.
  B. Manage resources, costs and liabilities to ensure the City’s long-term fiscal
  health.

ISSUE
Adopt Resolution No. CC 2020-122 Amending the City’s Classification and Pay Plans.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council adopt Resolution No. CC 2020-122 Amending
the City’s Classification and Pay Plans.

BACKGROUND
CalPERS requires that pay rates and schedules be duly approved and adopted by the
employer's governing body in accordance with requirements of applicable public
meetings laws. The minimum wage for the State of California is increasing from $13.00
per hour to $14.00 an hour effective January 1, 2021, thus the City needs to update the
existing pay schedules. The next and final increase will be to $15 per hour on January
1, 2022.

DISCUSSION
The City’s Classification and Pay Plans are being updated to comply with the new State
of California law increasing the minimum wage to $14.00 per hour. The proposed change
is effective January 1, 2021.

In addition, the Classification and Pay Plan for “Y” Rated Positions is being updated. Staff
no longer holds “Y” rated status for the Program Leader I classification therefore it is being
removed from the list. However, it will remain on the current Classification and Pay Plan
for Unbenefited Part-Time Positions in the Parks and Recreation Department.

FISCAL IMPACT
The increase in minimum wage is estimated to have a fiscal impact of approximately
$300,000 annually. However, due to the COVID-19 Pandemic restrictions, the impact

emergency to exist in California due to the spread of COVID-19. Following the March 4,
2020 declaration of a state of emergency, Governor Newsom and the Los Angeles
County Health Officer issued various Executive Orders and Public Health Orders
limiting in-person contact and activities, and temporarily restricting the operation of
restaurants and similar businesses; and,

  WHEREAS, Thereafter, the Orders were amended to allow for greater
occupancy within businesses, and allowed restaurants to resume operations outdoors;
and,

  WHEREAS, Many local businesses spent considerable time, money, and effort
to conform their businesses to the modified health Orders that provided for greater
occupancy and outdoor dining; and

  WHEREAS, On November 19, 2020, the Los Angeles County Public Health
Officer issued a Revised Order effective as of November 20, 2020, stating that indoor
operations for restaurants, breweries and wineries were to remain closed and in-person
outdoor dining may not be open between the hours of 10:00 p.m. and 6:00 a.m.; and,

  WHEREAS, On November 22, 2020, the Los Angeles Department of Public
Health announced the Health Officer Order will be modified to prohibit outdoor dining at
restaurants, breweries, wineries and bars effective Wednesday, November 25, 2020 at
10:00 p.m. for a minimum of three weeks; and,

  WHEREAS, These orders have had a devastating effect on local businesses,
including restaurants and breweries.

NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF
PALMDALE DOES HEREBY FIND, DETERMINE, RESOLVE AND ORDER AS

eliminating outdoor dining as the Orders lack a scientific nexus between the increased

BACKGROUND
In September 2020, the City of Palmdale submitted a grant for the SoCal Gas Climate
Adaptation & Resiliency Planning Grant Program to update the City’s FEMA-approved
LHMP. The City was informed November 9, 2020, that we were one of three applicants
who were awarded a grant in the amount of $50,000.

The Southern California Gas initiative is designed to support local efforts to prepare for
climate-change risks such as wildfires, drought, sea level rise, flooding, and other events,
which are expected to increase over the next decade. The winning applications were
selected from across Southern and Central California by an advisory panel of planning
and sustainability experts from the Los Angeles Regional Collaborative for Climate Action
and Sustainability (LARC)  and the American Planning Association-California
Chapter (APA-California). Recipients were chosen based on their proposal’s emphasis
on: collaboration among various agencies, first responders and utilities; addressing

  Palmdale Climate Resiliency Update to Local Hazard Mitigation Plan

1. Project Description
The City of Palmdale proposes a project to update the City’s FEMA-approved Local Hazard
Mitigation Plan (LHMP), with a specific focus on the climate risks, such as extreme heat,
wildfires, drought, subsidence, sea level rise, flooding and mudslides. This project will (1)
identify the City’s natural, environmental, and man-made challenges, with an emphasis on
identifying those hazards that will be exacerbated by climate change and (2) identify and
prioritize concrete, innovative, implementable climate change adaptation projects to incorporate
into the City’s emergency preparedness planning.
This project will produce an updated FEMA-approved LHMP for the City of Palmdale, with a
focus on innovative and implementable climate adaptation projects. The LHMP will offer an up-
to-date and comprehensive assessment of the risk and vulnerability from natural hazards to the
City’s critical facilities, infrastructure, economy, and population. The LHMP update will also
identify clear implementable projects to mitigate the identified hazards, the majority of which will
be impacted by climate change. Through a robust public engagement process, the updated
LHMP will reflect the needs and priorities of the community that the City serves.
This project is necessary to achieve a number of priorities for the City, including enhancing local
resilience to climate impacts; improving protection for critical infrastructure and vulnerable
communities as the City prepares for the impacts of climate change; and enhancing long-term
emergency management planning. This project will also allow the City to increase its climate
resilience in a way that addresses the City’s unique challenges, including its geographic
isolation from the majority of Los Angeles County and its challenging Mojave desert
environment, while at the same time being one of the fastest growing Cities in California.
This project will encompass planning for the entire City of Palmdale, which spans approximately
105 square miles in the Antelope Valley. The total expected cost for this project is $50,000
which includes the staff time costs for the members of City staff who will oversee the project, as
well as costs for the hiring of a qualified consultant to lead the planning process and to complete
the LHMP update. The start date for this project will be November 2020 and the project will be
completed by August 2022.

2. Project Justification
This project will directly address the issue of heightened climate risks that increase the City’s
vulnerability to natural disasters such as extreme heat, wildfires, drought, subsidence, sea level
rise, flooding and mudslides. The goal of this project is to enhance local resilience to climate
impacts; improve protection for critical infrastructure and vulnerable/disadvantaged communities
as the City prepares for the impacts of climate change; foster collaboration with stakeholders;
and enhance long-term emergency management planning. To specifically address the issue of
heightened climate risk issues and achieve these broader resiliency goals, this project will
facilitate a comprehensive update to the City’s FEMA-approved Local Hazard Mitigation Plan.
The LHMP update will focus on local hazards that will be exacerbated by climate change. The
LHMP will also offer an up-to-date and comprehensive assessment of the risk and vulnerability
from natural hazards to the City’s critical facilities, infrastructure, economy, and population.

3. Grant Specific Objectives
This project will meet Program criteria as follows:

  Effectively addresses the challenge of preparing a community for the impacts from
  climate change
This resilience planning effort will effectively prepare the Palmdale community for impacts form
climate change by identifying specific mitigation projects for implementation, which will fast track
future project implementation. Having a ready list of concreate projects that can be implemented
will facilitate implementation for these projects as future funding becomes available and will
ensure that the City is prepared. Additionally, this project will help protect a number of critical
facilities of national significance located in the City of Palmdale, including the United States Air
Force Plant 42, the NASA Armstrong Flight Research Center, and the Los Angeles Air Route
Traffic Control Center (ARTCC) that is operated by the Federal Aviation Administration.
These planning efforts will further ensure that the City is prepared to maintain the necessary
level of service at other critical local facilities in future emergencies resulting from climate
challenges such as flooding, extreme heat, and wildfire. This includes the South Antelope Valley
Emergency Services (SAVES) Building, which is critical City facility that serves the City’s most
vulnerable residents. Established in 1983, SAVES is the only local food pantry that serves very
low and extremely low-income individuals, working families, elderly, disabled, and homeless
residents in the entire south Antelope Valley. As such SAVES’ impact extends beyond the City
of Palmdale to surrounding communities, including Acton, Lake Elizabeth, Lake Los Angeles,
Littlerock, Llano, and Pearblossom. As the impacts of climate change and related challenges
expand in the coming years and decades, these impacts will most acutely affect the vulnerable
communities that SAVES serves. As such, the SAVES Building will continue serve as a regional
resource center for impacted communities and identifying that will improve the resilience of this
facility will ensure that the City is able to continue providing services even as climate change
presents new challenges.

  Supports low income communities/communities of color with limited resources?
This project will support low income communities and communities of color with limited
resources. The City of Palmdale as a whole is home to numerous disadvantaged at vulnerable
communities that this project will help protect. This includes low-income populations,
communities of color, and disadvantaged youth who may be particularly vulnerable to climate
change-exacerbated events such as drought, flooding, extreme heat, and wildfires.
The City of Palmdale is a majority-minority city, with historically underserved Latino/Hispanic
demographic group making up 58.6% of the population, and Black Americans making up 12.5%
of the population. Additionally, according to the most recently available figures from the U.S.
Census Bureau, more than 18% of the population lives in poverty, with median household
income is as low as $16,434 (Census Tract 06037910501, Department of Water Resources
DAC Mapping Tool) in some areas of the City. At the same time, many residents face disparate
health outcomes. According to the 2018 California Health Interview Survey and Southern
California Association of Governments (SCAG), the obesity rate in the City of Palmdale was
30.6%, higher than the County rate of 28.2%, while physical activity rate in much lower in the
City at 23.7% in comparison to the County at 39.2%.

An additional challenge in communities within the City includes a high proportion of youth
relative to the region as a whole; according to recent figures from the 2017 Los Angeles Public
Health Assessment, 41.3% of households in the City of Palmdale have children under the age
of 18 (one of the highest percentages in the County). Youth are particularly vulnerable to the
effects of climate change and, as the next generation of leaders and community members, will
bear an outsized proportion of the burden of climate change’s adverse impacts.
This project, by increasing the City’s resilience and preparedness for addressing climate
challenges, will directly benefit the City’s most vulnerable community members. Additionally,
through robust community engagement efforts, this project will support participation and
development of leadership in the City’s most disadvantaged communities. These efforts will
include interactive workshops and accessible public meetings that capture the input of the target
beneficiaries and stakeholders. Meeting notices, reports, and draft plans will be available to all
residents in multiple languages (at minimum, Spanish and English) and formats including print,
online via the City webpage for the project. The City will also engage partners for community
events and education efforts.

  Innovative, creative and encourages collaboration
As part of this project, the City will collaborate with a qualified private sector consultant for both
the LHMP update and development of the climate-focused EOP appendices. The City will select
the consultant through a Request For Proposals (RFP) process. After identifying implementation
projects through this planning process, the City will explore opportunities for private sector
innovation and collaboration in project implementation. Additionally, at this time, the focus of the
City’s proposed project will remain within the bounds of the City of Palmdale, but the City is
open to collaborating with neighboring jurisdictions on future implementation projects as
identified in the updated LHMP. The City’s goal is to identify creative and innovative mitigation
project for implementation as part of the planning process, which will facilitate future
collaboration.

  Identifies co-benefits of the adaptation work, such as benefits to public health, air
  quality, reductions in greenhouse gas emission, and the economy.
This project will achieve multiple benefits beyond increased climate resilience. These will
include improved emergency preparedness that specifically takes current and future
environmental conditions into consideration, expanded public education related to climate
change impacts and emergency preparedness, and improved understanding of the best
strategies to mitigate climate challenges at the local level. Additionally, while this project does
not focus specifically on greenhouse gas reduction measures, reduced greenhouse gas
emissions will likely be an additional benefit of the implementation projects identified through
this planning effort.

  Has existing partial funding that can be leveraged by a new grant & minimizes indirect
  administrative costs
At this time, the City has not secured any additional sources of funds for this project. The
requested funds will be sufficient to complete the entirety of the planning project proposed in
this application, and the resulting plan will position the City for success in pursuing future
implementation project funding. Moving forward, the City will be able to leverage any funds
awarded from this SoCal Gas grant as matching funds for future grant programs. To maximize

ISSUE
Adopt Resolution No. CC 2020-114 Authorizing Staff to Obtain On-Bill Financing Funds
from Southern California Edison.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Adopt Resolution No. CC 2020-114, authorizing staff to sign agreement number
  A-7251 with Southern California Edison to obtain a total of $116,202.56 in On-
  Bill Financing.

BACKGROUND
Recently, the City completed the retrofit of several lights located at Marie Kerr Park.
Although the primary concern with the lighting retrofits was to increase lighting levels at
the park, the City realized additional environmental and financial benefits. With the
assistance of The Energy Network, who provided assistance at no cost to the City, staff
submitted a request to Southern California Edison (SCE) to reserve On-Bill Financing
(OBF) funds to offset the cost of the project. OBF funds are provided at zero percent
interest and can be seen as an advance on anticipated savings.

Based on the retrofits performed, SCE calculates how much energy will be saved through
the retrofits and will provide loan funds. The term of the loan and required payments are
based on their calculations and will appear on the monthly bills received from SCE. As
an example, if SCE calculates that a retrofit will save a customer $100 per month, the
customer’s bill will remain the same as if the retrofits were not performed, but $100 of that
invoice will go to SCE as repayment on the loan. Then when the loan is paid off
completely, the customer will realize the full savings from the retrofit. The City has been
approved for a total of $116,202.56 in OBF funds. The loan repayment portion will be
$1,700.30 per month with a term of 69 months.

DISCUSSION
To reserve the funds, City staff had to submit a request to SCE. SCE is requiring the staff
member who requested the reservation of the funds sign the agreement on behalf of the
City. Therefore, staff is requesting the City Council approve a resolution authorizing the
execution of agreement number A-7251 with SCE for OBF funds and to authorize the
staff member who requested the reservation of the funds, Benjamin Lucha Environmental
& Technology Manager, to sign the agreements on behalf of the City.

FISCAL IMPACT
As a result of the Light Emitting Diode (LED) lighting retrofits performed at Marie Kerr
Park, the City has been approved by SCE to receive OBF funds in the amount of
$116,202.56. The funds are based on anticipated savings from the retrofits and the
monthly payments will appear on SCE invoices for accounts affected by the retrofits. The
loan should have no effect on the energy invoices paid by Marie Kerr Park until the loan
is paid in its entirety, when the City will realize all of the savings anticipated by the retrofits.

  Program Description
  The On-Bill Financing (OBF) program is offered by Southern California Edison Company (SCE) to qualified SCE
  non-residential service customers and multi-family property customers (Customer) to offset the cost of purchasing
  and installing eligible energy efficiency equipment (Solutions). Through OBF, qualified Customers will receive zero
  percent (0%) interest, no-fee, unsecured financing for Solutions for which incentives and rebates are approved under
  an eligible SCE energy efficiency program (Eligible Program).1
  Financing is available to qualified Customers for up to one hundred percent (100%) of the actual installed cost (up to
  the amount approved by SCE) of approved Solutions, less rebates or incentives received by Customer from SCE
  under applicable Eligible Program(s).2 The minimum loan amount per service account available through OBF is five
  thousand dollars ($5,000). The maximum OBF loan amount available per service account is (i) two hundred fifty
  thousand dollars ($250,000) for government and institutional taxpayer-funded and multi-family property Customers,
  and (ii) one hundred thousand dollars ($100,000) for commercial Customers3, including general business, industrial
  and agricultural entities.
  Customers may qualify for multiple loans under OBF provided the aggregate dollar amount of the loans does not
  exceed the maximum OBF loan amount per service account stated above.4
  The maximum loan term for a taxpayer-funded government, institutional and multi-family property Customer is ten
  (10) years (or the expected useful life 5 of the Installed Solutions, whichever is shorter). The maximum loan term for a

ISSUE
Adopt Resolutions No.’s CC 2020-111 and CC 2020-112 initiating proceedings for the
approval of the annexation, approving the preliminary Engineer’s Report, and
declaring the City’s intention to levy and collect assessments within Palmdale
Streetlight Maintenance Assessment District No. 1, Annexation 2020-193 for Fiscal
year 2021/2022.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council adopt Resolutions No.’s CC 2020-111 and CC
2020-112 approving the preliminary Engineer’s Report and declaring the City’s
intention to levy and collect assessments for this annexation into Palmdale Streetlight
Maintenance Assessment District No. 1.

BACKGROUND
As a condition of approval for the project, Edwards Federal Credit Union, located at
39963 10th Street West, streetlight improvements are required. Edwards Federal
Credit Union, the owner, is required to install all of the necessary streetlight
improvements for the proposed Edwards Federal Credit Union site.

According to the “Landscaping and Lighting Act of 1972”, Part 2 of Division 15 of the
California Streets and Highways Code, the City may establish a streetlight

maintenance assessment district or annex territory into an existing district to provide
for the installation, continued maintenance, and servicing of the streetlight
improvements. Placement of the streetlight improvements into a district will provide for
the continued maintenance of these improvements after the developer installs them
and the City accepts them.

Article XIII D of the California Constitution, and Section 53753 of the California
Government Code both require that a notice of the proposed assessment and ballot be
mailed to the record owner of each parcel on which an assessment is imposed.
Additionally, the Article requires that the City conduct a public hearing no earlier than
45 days from the date of approval of the Resolution of Intention.

At this time Edwards Federal Credit Union, is the sole owner of Assessor Parcel
Number 3005-050-001, covering the territory located at 39963 10th Street West. The
owner has been mailed a petition requesting the owner to waive the 45-day notice
period thereby shortening the time between the Resolution of Intention and the public
hearing. A ballot will also be mailed to the owner, to indicate their support or
opposition to the annexation of the Palmdale Streetlight Maintenance Assessment
District No. 1, Annexation 2020-193.

The City has prepared resolutions initiating proceedings to approve the annexation of
the Assessment District, and to levy and collect assessments to fund the cost of
maintenance of streetlight improvements within the Assessment District. The City
Council has designated the assessment engineer and will hear on the preliminary
report, which outlines the Assessment District and the proposed annual assessments.

The attached resolutions and Engineer’s Report initiate the process for the annexation
of the Assessment District and set a date for the public hearing. At the time of the
public hearing, the ballot will be checked, and if the vote is yes, the Engineer’s Report
and resolution to be heard at the public hearing will confirm and levy assessments
placed upon each parcel for the operation, maintenance and servicing costs.

DISCUSSION
Approval of Palmdale Streetlight Maintenance Assessment District No. 1, Annexation
2020-193 will provide for the continued maintenance, and servicing of streetlight
improvements, in the Annexation area, after the developer installs them and the City
accepts them.

Maintenance Assessment District No. 1, Annexation 2020-193, Edwards Federal

INTRODUCTION

  BACKGROUND
  The City of Palmdale (the “City”) provides maintenance and servicing of certain publicly
  owned street and traffic lights throughout the City. In order to fund the maintenance and
  operation (the “Services”) of these projects and improvements (the “Improvements”), the
  City has formed five Streetlight Maintenance Assessment Districts, including subsequent
  annexations, covering an area of approximately 26,000 acres and about 41,000 parcels.
  These assessment districts have been formed and the levies have been made pursuant to
  Part 2 of Division 15 of the California Streets and Highways Code, commonly known as the
  Landscape and Lighting Act of 1972 (the “Act”), and Article XIIID of the California
  Constitution (the “Article”).

  In September 2020, the property owner, Edwards Federal Credit Union (and Level 5, the
  developer), requested the formation of a streetlight maintenance assessment district
  associated with the frontage improvements of a future 14,118 square foot commercial
  building (Credit Union and offices) to be built on Assessor Parcel Number 3005-050-001.
  This property is located at 39963 10th Street West in Palmdale. After consultation with City
  staff, the decision was made to create a new streetlight assessment district for this project.

  The Palmdale Streetlight Maintenance Assessment District No. 1 (“District”), Annexation
  2020-193 (the “Assessment District” or “Annexation”), is proposed to include funding for the
  maintenance and operation of street lights, traffic lights, and related improvements
  (“Improvements and Services”) that benefit the Edwards Federal Credit Union property that
  forms the Assessment District. The property proposed to be included in the Assessment
  District consists of 14,118 square foot commercial building consisting of a Credit Union and
  offices to be built on 1.61 acres within the City of Palmdale.

  The developer proposes to construct frontage improvements along the south side of Avenue
  O-8 and east side of 10th Street West. This Assessment District annexation, described in
  this Engineer’s Report, results from agreements or conditions of approval between the City
  of Palmdale and the property owner, Edwards Federal Credit Union, whereby the City and
  the property owner agreed on the maintenance and operation of the additional street lights
  to enhance the safety, utility, and access of the property within the Assessment District.

  ENGINEER’S REPORT
  This Engineer’s Report (“Report”) was prepared to establish the budget for the services that
  would be funded by the proposed 2021/2022 assessment, to determine the benefits received
  from the maintenance and operation of the additional street lights within the Assessment
  District, and to define the method of assessment apportionment to lots and parcels. This
  Report and the proposed assessments have been prepared pursuant to the Landscape and
  Lighting Act of 1972, Part 2 of Division 15 of the California Streets and Highways Code and
  Article XIIID of the California Constitution.

  LEGISLATIVE ANALYSIS
  PROPOSITION 218
  The Right to Vote on Taxes Act was approved by the voters of California on November 6,
  1996, and is now Article XIIIC and XIIID of the California Constitution. Proposition 218
  provides for benefit assessments to be levied to fund the cost of providing services,
  improvements, as well as maintenance and operation expenses to a public improvement
  which benefits the assessed property. This Assessment District will be balloted and
  approved by property owners in accordance with Proposition 218.

  SILICON VALLEY TAXPAYERS ASSOC., INC. V SANTA CLARA COUNTY OPEN SPACE AUTHORITY
  In July of 2008, the California Supreme Court issued its ruling on the Silicon Valley
  Taxpayers Association, Inc. vs. Santa Clara County Open Space Authority (SVTA). This
  ruling is the most significant court case in further legally clarifying the substantive
  assessment requirements of Proposition 218. Several of the most important elements of the
  ruling included further emphasis that:

    Benefit assessments are for special benefits to property, not general benefits.
    The services and/or improvements funded by assessments must be clearly defined.
    Assessment districts must be drawn to contain all parcels that receive a special
  benefit from a proposed public improvement.
    Assessments paid in the assessment district must be proportional to the special
  benefit received by each such parcel from the improvements and services funded
  by the assessment.

  This Engineer’s Report and the process used to establish these proposed assessments for
  fiscal year 2021/2022 are consistent with the SVTA decision and with the requirements of
  Article XIIIC and XIIID of the California Constitution based on the following factors:

  1. The Assessment District is narrowly drawn to include only the properties that receive
  special benefit from the specific Improvements and Services. Thus, zones of benefit
  are not required, and the assessment revenue derived from real property in each
  Assessment District is extended only on the Services in the Assessment District.

  2. The Improvements which are constructed and/or maintained with assessment proceeds
  in the Assessment District are located in close proximity to the real property subject to
  the assessment. The Improvements and Services provide illumination to streets and
  sidewalks enabling improved access to the owners, residents, and guests of such
  assessed property. The proximity of the Improvements to the assessed parcels and the
  improved access and increased safety provided to the residents of the assessed parcels
  by the Improvements, provides a special benefit to the parcels being assessed pursuant
  to the factors outlined by the Supreme Court in that decision.

  3. Due to their proximity to the assessed parcels, the Improvements and Services financed
  with assessment revenues in the Assessment District benefit the properties in the
  Assessment District in a manner different in kind from the benefit that other parcels of
  real property in the City derive from such Improvements and Services, and the benefits
  conferred on such property in the Assessment District are more extensive than a general
  increase in property values.

  4. The assessments paid in the Assessment District are proportional to the special benefit
  that each parcel within the Assessment District receives from the Services because:

  DAHMS V. DOWNTOWN POMONA PROPERTY
  On June 8, 2009, the 4th Court of Appeal amended its original opinion upholding a benefit
  assessment for property in the downtown area of the City of Pomona (“Dahms”). On July
  22, 2009, the California Supreme Court denied review. On this date, Dahms became good
  law and binding precedent for assessments. In Dahms the Court upheld an assessment
  that was 100% special benefit (i.e. 0% general benefit) on the rationale that the services and
  improvements funded by the assessments were directly provided to property in the
  assessment district. The Court also upheld discounts and exemptions from the assessment
  for certain properties.

  BONANDER V. TOWN OF TIBURON
  On December 31, 2009, the 1st District Court of Appeal overturned a benefit assessment
  approved by property owners to pay for placing overhead utility lines underground in an area
  of the Town of Tiburon (“Bonander”). The Court invalidated the assessments on the grounds
  that the assessments had been apportioned to assessed property based in part on relative
  costs within sub-areas of the assessment district instead of proportional special benefits.

  BEUTZ V. COUNTY OF RIVERSIDE
  On May 26, 2010 the 4th District Court of Appeal issued a decision on the Steven Beutz v.
  County of Riverside (“Beutz”) appeal. This decision overturned an assessment for park
  maintenance in Wildomar, California, primarily because the general benefits associated with
  improvements and services were not explicitly calculated, quantified and separated from the
  special benefits.

  GOLDEN HILL NEIGHBORHOOD ASSOCIATION V. CITY OF SAN DIEGO
  On September 22, 2011, the San Diego Court of Appeal issued a decision on the Golden
  Hill Neighborhood Association v. City of San Diego appeal. This decision overturned an
  assessment for street and landscaping maintenance in the Greater Golden Hill
  neighborhood of San Diego, California (“Greater Golden Hill”). The court described two
  primary reasons for its decision. First, like in Beutz, the court found the general benefits
  associated with services were not explicitly calculated, quantified and separated from the
  special benefits. Second, the court found that the City had failed to record the basis for the
  assessment on its own parcels.

  advantage to property in the Assessment District that would not be received in absence of
  the Assessments.

  This Engineer’s Report is consistent with Beutz, Dahms and Greater Golden Hill because
  the Improvements and Services will directly benefit property in the Assessment District and
  the general benefits have been excluded from the Assessments. The Engineer’s Report is
  consistent with Bonander because the Assessments have been apportioned based on the
  overall cost of the Improvements and Services and proportional special benefit to each
  property.

METHOD OF ASSESSMENT

  ASSESSMENT METHODOLOGY
  This section of the Engineer’s Report includes an explanation of the benefits to be derived
  from the Improvements and Services throughout the Assessment District and the
  Assessment methodology used to apportion the total Assessment to properties within the
  Assessment District.

  The Assessment District consist of all assessor parcels within the boundaries, as defined by
  the Assessment Diagram included with this report, and the parcels identified by the Assessor
  Parcel Numbers listed in the assessment roll, also included in this report. The parcel list
  includes all privately and publicly owned parcels within the boundaries. The method used for
  apportioning the Assessment is based on the proportional special benefits to be derived by
  the properties in the Assessment District, over and above general benefits conferred on real
  property or to the public at large. The apportionment of special benefit is a two-step process:
  the first step is to identify the types of special benefit arising from the Improvements and
  Services, and the second step is to allocate the Assessments to property based on the
  estimated relative special benefit for each type of property.

  DISCUSSION OF BENEFIT
  The Assessments can only be levied based on the special benefit to property. This special
  benefit is received by a property over and above any general benefit. The assessments are
  levied upon those parcels within an identified Assessment District where the Improvements
  and Services provided are specific to those parcels. Moreover, such a benefit is not based
  on any one property owner’s use of the Improvements and Services or a property owner’s
  specific demographic status. With reference to the requirements for Assessments, Section
  22573 of the Act states:

  “The net amount to be assessed upon lands within an assessment district
  may be apportioned by any formula or method which fairly distributes the
  net amount among all assessable lots or parcels in proportion to the
  estimated benefits to be received by each such lot or parcel from the
  improvements.”

  Proposition 218, as codified in Article XIIID of the California Constitution, has confirmed that
  Assessments must be based on the special benefit to property:

  No assessment shall be imposed on any parcel which exceeds the
  reasonable cost of the proportional special benefit conferred on that parcel.

  The following benefit categories summarize the types of special benefit to residential,
  commercial, industrial, and other lots and parcels resulting from the Services. These
  categories of special benefit are derived in part from the statues passed by the California
  Legislature and other studies which describe the types of special benefit received by the

    Proximity to Improvements within the Assessment District.
    Improved safety and security lighting for property.
    Improved ingress and egress to property for vehicular traffic and pedestrians.
    Creation of individual lots for development or approval of building permits that in the

  The recent Silicon Valley Taxpayers Association, Inc. vs. Santa Clara County Open Space
  Authority (SVTA) decision provides enhanced clarity to the definition of special benefits to
  property based on the proximity of the Improvements and Services.

  The SVTA decision also clarifies that a special benefit is a service or improvement that
  provides a direct advantage to a parcel, and that indirect or derivative advantages resulting
  from the overall public benefits from a service or improvement are general benefits. The
  SVTA decision also provides specific guidance that improvements that are proximate to
  property are a direct advantage and special benefit to property:

  “the characterization of a benefit may depend on whether the parcel
  receives a direct advantage from the improvement (e.g. proximity to a park)
  or receives an indirect, derivative advantage resulting from the overall
  public benefits of the improvement (e.g. general enhancement of the
  district’s property values).”

  Proximity, in addition to the other special benefits listed above, further strengthens the basis
  of this assessment.

  BENEFIT FACTORS
  The special benefits from the Improvements and Services are further detailed below:

  PROXIMITY TO IMPROVEMENTS WITHIN THE ASSESSMENT DISTRICT
  Only the specific properties within close proximity to the Improvements and Services are
  included in the Assessment District. Therefore, property in the Assessment District enjoys
  unique and valuable proximity to the Improvements that the public at large and property
  outside the Assessment District do not share.

  In absence of the assessments, the Improvements and Services would not be provided and
  would be degraded or inoperable due to insufficient funding for maintenance, upkeep and
  repair. Therefore, the assessments provide Improvements and Services that are over and
  above what otherwise would be provided. Improvements and Services that are over and
  above what otherwise would be provided do not by themselves translate into special benefits
  but, when combined with the unique proximity enjoyed by parcels in the Assessment District,
  they provide a direct advantage and special benefit to property in the Assessment District.

  illumination also serves to deter criminal activity during hours of dusk and darkness. This is
  a direct advantage and special benefit to the property in the Assessment District.

  IMPROVED INGRESS AND EGRESS TO PROPERTY FOR VEHICULAR TRAFFIC AND PEDESTRIANS
  The Improvements and Services provide illumination to streets and sidewalks in and
  immediately adjacent to the Assessment District. This illumination allows improved ingress
  and egress to the parcels within the Assessment District and reduces the potential for
  accidents and property damage. This is a direct advantage and special benefit to the
  property in the Assessment District.

  CREATION OF INDIVIDUAL LOTS FOR DEVELOPMENT OR APPROVAL OF BUILDING PERMITS THAT IN
  ABSENCE OF THE ASSESSMENTS WOULD NOT HAVE BEEN CREATED OR APPROVED
  The developer or the owner of the property at the time of development agreed to the
  assessments. As parcels were sold, new owners were informed of the assessments through
  the title reports, and in some cases, through Department of Real Estate “White Paper”
  reports that the parcels were subject to assessment. Purchase of property was also an
  “agreement” to pay the assessment. Moreover, in absence of the assessments, the lots
  within the Assessment Districts would not have been created or building permits would not
  have been approved. These lots, and the Improvements they support, are a special benefit
  to the property owners.

  GENERAL VERSUS SPECIAL BENEFIT
  The proceeds from Streetlight Maintenance Assessment District No. 1, Annexation 2020-
  193, are used to fund Improvements and increased levels of maintenance to the public
  facilities that serve and benefit the properties in the Assessment District. In absence of the
  Streetlight Maintenance Assessment District No. 1, Annexation 2020-193, such
  Improvements would not be properly maintained. Therefore, the Assessment District’s
  purpose is to ensure that the necessary and beneficial public facilities for property in the
  Assessment District are properly maintained and repaired over time. The assessments will
  ensure that street lighting and associated improvements within and adjacent to the
  Assessment District are functional, well maintained and safe. These public resources

  conferred exclusively on property in the Assessment District and not enjoyed by other
  properties outside the Assessment District. Therefore, the assessments solely provide

  QUANTIFICATION OF GENERAL BENEFIT
  Although the analysis used to support these assessments concludes that the benefits are
  solely special, as described above, consideration is made for the suggestion that a portion

  funding must come from other sources.

  The maintenance and servicing of these improvements is also partially funded, directly and
  indirectly from other sources including the City of Palmdale, Los Angeles County, and the
  State of California. This funding comes in the form of grants, development fees, special
  programs, and general funds, as well as direct maintenance and servicing of facilities (e.g.
  curbs, gutters, streets, drainage systems, etc.). This funding from other sources more than
  compensates for general benefits, if any, received by the properties within the Assessment
  District.

  In the 2009 Dahms case, the court upheld an assessment that was 100% special benefit on
  the rationale that the services funded by the assessments were directly provided within the
  assessment district. It is also important to note that the improvements and services funded

  Assessments described in this Engineer’s Report, and the Court found these improvements

  ASSESSMENT METHODOLOGY
  The second step in apportioning assessments is to determine the relative special benefit for
  each property. The Assessment Districts and Annexations assessments are based on land
  use to ensure properties are assessed in proportion to the benefits received. The land uses
  defined below are descriptive of all potential parcels. This process involves determining the
  relative benefit received by each property in relation to a single-family home, or, in other
  words, on the basis of Equivalent Dwelling Units (EDUs). This EDU methodology is
  commonly used to distribute assessments in proportion to estimated special benefit and is
  generally recognized as providing the basis for a fair and appropriate distribution of
  assessments. For the purposes of this Engineer’s Report, all properties are designated an
  EDU value, which is each property’s relative benefit in relation to a single-family home on
  one parcel. In this case, the "benchmark" property is the single-family detached dwelling
  which is one Equivalent Dwelling Unit or one EDU.

  A.  Developer proposes developing a 31-unit multifamily rental housing project on
certain real property located at the southwest corner of Ninth Street East and Avenue Q-11 in the

permanent loan from an institutional lender, Developer Equity, a construction to permanent loan
from the Authority of Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Funds (“LMIHAF”), or alternative
financing proposed by Developer and approved by the Authority.

Agreement, and the fulfillment generally of this Agreement are in the vital and best interests of the
City of Palmdale and the health, safety and welfare of its residents, and in accord with the public
purposes and provisions of applicable federal, state and local laws and requirements.

agree as follows:

  METHOD OF FINANCING

This is the Method of Financing attached to the Affordable Housing Agreement dated as of
December 15, 2020, between the Housing Authority of the City of Palmdale (“Authority”) and
Ninth Patriot LLC (“Developer”), relating to Developer’s construction of a 31-unit multifamily
housing project (including one manager’s unit), of which four units are to be rented, at
Affordable Rents, to Very Low Income households.

The Project’s Development Costs will be financed by a combination of a Senior Loan, the
Authority Loan, and Developer Equity. Developer may utilize alternative or additional financing
sources approved by the Authority Executive Director, so long as such other financing does not
impose an additional burden on the Authority or the City of Palmdale.

The Authority Loan is in the principal amount of $900,000. The Authority Loan will be funded
during the Construction Period and will convert to permanent financing at Conversion. The
Authority Loan will be repaid during the Permanent Period from Residual Receipts according to
the terms and conditions of the Authority Note.

  1.  Definitions. Any capitalized term not otherwise defined herein has the meaning
ascribed to such term in the Affordable Housing Agreement.

  2.  Total Development Costs. The parties estimate that the total Development Costs
for the Project will be approximately $7,659,906.

  3.  Sources of Construction Financing.

The Parties anticipate that the Development Costs for the Project will be financed during the
Construction Period with the following combinations of funds. Developer must make every
reasonable effort to structure the terms of the construction financing in a way that will minimize
the amount of the Authority Loan needed to fill the financing gap.

  (a) The Construction Loan, in the approximate original principal amount of
  $5,361,714, to be secured by a first deed of trust.

  (b)  The Authority Loan in the original principal amount of $900,000.

  (c)  Costs deferred to Conversion, consisting of deferred funding of reserves in
  the amount of $0.

  (d) Developer Equity consisting of advances and capital contributions made
  by Developer’s Managing Member in the approximate amount of
  $1,398,192.

  (e)  Developer will be responsible during the Construction Period to provide
  funds if and as needed to pay for cost overruns and contingencies not
  otherwise funded by the sources of funds as described herein.

  4.  Sources of Permanent Financing.

The Parties anticipate that the Development Costs of the Project will be financed during the
Permanent Period with the following combinations of funds. Developer must make every
reasonable effort to structure the terms of the permanent financing in a way that will minimize
the amount of the Authority Loan needed to fill the financing gap.

  (a)  The Permanent Loan, in the approximate original principal amount of
  $5,361,714, to be secured by a first priority deed of trust;

  (b)  The Authority Loan described in paragraph 3(b) above in the original
  principal amount of $900,000;

  (c)  Developer Equity, consisting of the capital contributions described in
  paragraph 3(d) above in the approximate amount of $1,398,192.

  5.  Project Budget. The Parties anticipate that all Development Costs for the Project
will be as set forth in the Project Budget attached to the Affordable Housing Agreement as
Attachment No. 6. The Project Budget will be subject to change from time to time, subject to the

be unreasonably withheld) and subject to and conditioned on such further review and approval
by the Authority Board of Commissioners as is needed to satisfy applicable law and Authority
policies and procedures, upon which approval the Project Budget will be replaced by the
approved revised Project Budget. Within the time provided in the Schedule of Performance, the

  SCOPE OF DEVELOPMENT

1.  General

  The Project will consist of 31 two-bedroom units of multifamily housing to be developed on
the Property. Each unit will be at least 1,425 square feet. Each residential unit will have individual
heating and cooling controls, separate living, eating, sleeping, bathroom and cooking areas, and
private patios or balconies. The Project’s common areas will include picnic tables and barbeque grill.
All required parking will be provided on-site.

  The Project will be designed and developed to promote safety and accessibility for residents
and their guests. The code-required number of units will be fully handicapped accessible (See #4,
below).

  The Project will be planned to promote “natural surveillance” of parking, pathways and other
common areas and of entrances to individual residential units. Exterior lighting will be provided to
offer the greatest degree of security without intruding into adjacent properties. The Developer shall
participate in the City of Palmdale’s and Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department’s Partners
Against Crime (“PAC”) program, and any equivalent substitute program that is created to replace the
PAC program. Developer’s obligations under the PAC program include assuring that the Project’s
property managers receive PAC training and maintain PAC certification throughout the life of the
Project.

  The plans and specifications for the Project will be subject to the Housing Authority’s
approval. Development of the Property in accordance with this Agreement is subject to the City of
Palmdale Planning Commission and City Council approval, the City’s post approval plan check, the
issuance of permits and all other applicable City of Palmdale entitlement, approval, and permit
requirements.

2.  Standards, Controls and Restrictions

  Standards, controls and restrictions regarding construction and development including, but
not limited to, maximum lot coverage, setbacks, and building construction will be as required by the
General Plan and Palmdale Municipal Code (PMC), and will be as mutually agreed upon by the
Housing Authority and Developer in the approved construction drawings, plans and specifications,
and will be consistent with the approved conceptual development standards and the Site Plan Review
plans and standards, including conditions of approval. The following standards will apply to the
Project.

  307
 Affordable Housing Agreement  Agreement No. A-6987

  a.  Architectural Standards

  The architecture of all structures shall maintain a high quality of design and establish visual
continuity with existing and proposed developments surrounding the Property.

  (1)  Form and Scale

  The structures on the Property shall combine a form and scale which are
  compatible with the adjoining land uses and the street environment.

  (2)  Street Level Design

  The facade as seen from the street shall be such that the shape, exterior
  design and exterior finish of the structures are consonant with and visually
  related to each other and surrounding developments.

  (3)  Building Materials

  Building materials shall be subject to the Housing Authority’s and Planning
  Commission approval.

  (4)  Sustainability

  Energy efficient features shall be incorporated into the design of the
  development including passive energy conservation methods. The Developer
  will be required to demonstrate consideration of energy features as a part of
  the design review and building permit process. Specifically, the Project shall
  utilize Energy Star certified appliances exceeding California Code of
  Regulations Title 24 standards by at least 15%. Water-efficient landscaping
  in compliance with PMC Section 14.05 will be used throughout the Project.
  The Developer will be required to demonstrate that the Project is solar and
  electric vehicle ready.

  b.  Siting and Land Use Standards

  (1)  Building Location

  The location of the building shall relate to and take advantage of
  developments and attractions surrounding the Property. All buildings will
  meet the setbacks required by the PMC.

  308
 Affordable Housing Agreement  Agreement No. A-6987
Ninth Patriot LLC  Attachment No. 5 – Scope of Development
APN: 3009-018-009 thru -016  Page 3

  (2)  Building Height

  Maximum building height shall be 34 feet.

  (3)  Views

  The structures shall be sited to minimize the impact on the views from
  existing and proposed structures surrounding the Property. To the extent
  possible, structures shall face open space.

  (4)  Open Space

  Patios, plazas, gardens and other pedestrian oriented common open spaces
  shall be located throughout the Project meeting the minimum 15% of the lot
  area and with as much open space as practicable in areas where greater use
  will be encouraged. A minimum of 150 feet of private open space is required.
  The unit design includes a deck on the 2 nd and 3rd levels.

  (5)  Rooftops

  On all buildings whose roof is visible from surrounding structures or
  proposed structures, pedestrian ways, streets, etc., exposed duct work for
  heating and cooling, mechanical equipment and other roof structures shall be
  screened from the direct view of adjacent property or buildings by the
  building parapets or in a manner approved by the Housing Authority and the
  Planning Commission.

  (6)  Parking

  All parking for the Project shall be located within the boundaries of the
  Property.

  c.  Streetscape Design Standards

  (1)  Landscaping

  Developer shall provide and maintain landscaping within setback areas along
  all street frontages. All landscaping shall be integrated with the existing or
  proposed landscaping for adjacent sites in the Project area. Landscaping
  includes such materials as paving, trees, shrubs, and other plant materials,

 Affordable Housing Agreement  Agreement No. A-6987

the Property, which will provide thirty-one (31) two-bedroom residential rental units and associated

  a.  Owner covenants and agrees for itself, its successors, its assigns and every
successor in interest to the Property or any part thereof, that Owner, its successors and assignees will
use the Property exclusively to provide 31 units of rental housing, including one two-bedroom

“Affordable Units”). The household incomes of eligible occupants of the Affordable Units will be
determined in accordance with section 6914 of Title 25 of the California Code of Regulations and
must not exceed fifty percent (50%) of Area Median Income, adjusted for family size. The term
“Area Median Income” means the area median income for Los Angeles County as published
annually by California’s Housing and Community Development Department pursuant to Health and
Safety Code section 50093. All of the Affordable Units must be rented exclusively to Very Low
Income Households at an Affordable Rent as provided in California Health and Safety Code section
50053.

  b.  Immediately prior to a prospective tenant’s occupancy of an Affordable Unit,
Owner will obtain and maintain on file an income computation and certification in a form provided
by the Authority and dated immediately prior to the date of initial occupancy. Owner will verify that
the income information provided by the applicant is accurate by following all applicable Authority
policies and procedures and by taking the following steps as a part of the verification process: (i)
obtain two (2) pay stubs from the most recent pay periods; (ii) obtain a written verification of income
and employment from applicant’s current employer; (iii) obtain an income verification form from the
Social Security Administration and/or California Department of Social Services if the applicant
receives assistance from either agency; (iv) if an applicant is unemployed or did not file a tax return
for the previous calendar year, obtain other verification of such applicant’s income as is reasonably
satisfactory; or (v) obtain such other information as may be reasonably required. Owner must update
the foregoing records annually and provide copies of updated tenant eligibility records and monthly
rental records to the Authority for review. Upon review of such records, the Authority may at its
option perform an independent audit of the tenant eligibility records in order to verify compliance
with the income and affordability requirements set forth herein. Costs for such an audit performed
by the Authority will be deemed an Operating Expense deductible from the Project’s Revenue (as

The future arrival of the California High Speed Rail system, including a multi-modal rail
station near the existing Palmdale Transportation Center, will transform the way residents
live, work and recreate in the City of Palmdale. High speed rail service to the San
Fernando Valley and the City of Los Angeles will provide additional travel options for
commuters. When combined with expanded Metrolink, Amtrak, Greyhound and Antelope
Valley Transit Authority bus service, and improvements to key arterials and freeways, the
expanded rail service will help reduce congestion, air pollution, and provide better travel
options for residents.
Planning for the arrival of high-speed rail in Palmdale began over 20 years ago and
continues in anticipation of its arrival. The City has been studying transit-oriented
development which involves the creation of vibrant, walkable, pedestrian-oriented, mixed-
use communities centered around train systems. Transit-oriented development reduces
dependence on personal vehicles which in turn reduces energy consumption and
greenhouse gas emissions, which then has a positive correlation to climate change. Two
of the planning studies that have been completed in preparation for the future multi-modal
high-speed rail station are as follows:
    Avenue Q Feasibility Study (2016) – The study area encompassed properties to
  the north and south of Avenue Q between Division Street and the western terminus
  of Avenue Q, an area that will act as a corridor into the future multi-modal high-
  speed rail station. The intent of the study was to plan for a transit-oriented, mixed-
  use corridor and includes standards and design guidelines for the streetscape and
  future development.
    Transit-Oriented Development (TOD3) Land Use Framework Plan (2018) – The
  study area is generally bound by Rancho Vista Boulevard to the north, 10th Street
  East to the east, Palmdale Boulevard to the south and State Route 14 to the west.
  This plan created the foundation, including broad-level environmental clearance,
  for all future transit-oriented development within the plan area, including
  SPL 20-001.
A third study, funded by the Southern California Association of Governments (SCAG), is
currently in the beginning stages. The intent of the study is to evaluate a complete streets
corridor on Avenue Q from 20th Street East to Sierra Highway, which will focus on
providing multi-modal connectivity to the future high-speed rail station is underway. The
study is anticipated to be completed in 2021-2022.
This proposed project was facilitated by a grant funded by the California High Speed Rail
Authority (CHSRA). The grant was intended to be used for creation of a comprehensive
plan that incentivizes and facilitates development specifically geared toward multi-modal
transit associated with the future multi-modal high-speed rail station. In addition to high-
speed rail, some of the transit carriers that are envisioned to utilize the future multi-modal
high-speed rail station are Brightline, Metrolink, Amtrak, Greyhound and Antelope Valley
Transit Authority.

The draft PTASP has been created in collaboration with CHSRA, stakeholders and the
community. Given that the development envisioned within the PTASP is transit-oriented
and the concepts within the document are not utilized within any existing developments
within the City, staff recognized the need to create a comprehensive outreach plan to
ensure as much input was received as possible. As such, over the course of time from
2016 until 2020, the following engagement activities have occurred:
    Stakeholder interviews with representatives from:
  o Local schools;
  o The aerospace industry;
  o Local business owners;
  o Medical professionals;
  o LA Metro;
  o Metrolink;
  o Union Pacific Railroad;
  o CHSRA;
  o Private landowners; and,
  o Southern California Association of Governments.
    Mobile visioning workshops to solicit input from local 8th and 10th grade students
  at the Palmdale Aerospace Academy in May 2016;
    Online survey from August 2016 until February 2017;
    Public workshops held at Yucca Elementary School and City Hall:
  o April 2016;
  o November 2016;
  o October 2017;
  o August 2019; and,
  o October 2019.
Some of the key comments and concerns received during the outreach period were as
follows:
    Avoidance of gentrification and displacement of residents;
    Concern regarding sharp increases in property values with development of the
  future multi-modal high-speed rail station;
    Create a destination/experience/sense of place around the future multi-modal
  high-speed rail station; and,
    Ensure safety, ease of access, convenience and walkability.
In addition, the development community weighed in on the PTASP and some of the key
comments and concerns received were as follows:
    Create a development document that includes form-based zoning;
    Development opportunities preferred on land that has already  been
  environmentally cleared; and,
    Streamline approval, permitting and inspection processes.

In conjunction with public outreach, a Technical Working Group (TWG) consisting of
approximately 30 members representing broad cross-sections of the community held
eight meetings between March 2016 and June 2019. The TWG was established to:
    Serve as a collaborative discussion forum to evaluate key concepts at a draft level;
    Provide input and feedback on concepts developed for the future multi-modal high-
  speed rail station area plan; and,
    Act as a forum to communicate progress made and agreements reached to TWG
  member constituents.
The TWG created the following vision statement:
“The Palmdale high-speed rail station area will be a gateway to the 21st Century for the
City of Palmdale, bringing together people from Palmdale, the region and the
southwestern states, celebrating a lifestyle that embraces the union of transportation,
community, and the environment. It will be a vibrant mixed-use center that embodies the
sustainable, physical, economic and social development of the area and be the catalyst
for a more dynamic diverse and livable Palmdale.”
Some of the key discussions occurring during the TWG meetings included:
    The overall vision for the area surrounding the future multi-modal high-speed rail
  station;
    Rail alignment;
    Multi-modal access and circulation within and around the area; and,
    Traditional zoning regulations versus form-based regulations.

Specific Plan Amendment
SPA 20-001 is a request to amend the eastern boundary of the PT&CCSP to remove the
portion of the plan bound by Technology Drive to the north, Division Street to the east,
Palmdale Boulevard to the south and State Route 14 to the west. As proposed, this area

State Route 14. In addition, as proposed within the PTASP, future development in this
area would support the envisioned higher density and intensity of developments located
to the east, which is closer to the future multi-modal high-speed rail station.
Specific Plan
SPL 20-001 (PTASP) is intended to provide a comprehensive master plan for
development in the vicinity of the existing and future multi-modal high-speed rail station.
The specific plan outlines area specific designations, development standards, design
guidelines and methods for implementation and provides future developers with flexibility
while ensuring cohesive development of the specific plan area. Due to the unique
character envisioned for the specific plan area, creation of a traditional zoning map for
the PTASP would not achieve the desired result. As such, a regulating plan was created
to control the design and placement of new development in a manner that addresses the
size and mass of buildings in relation to one another (FIGURE 4).

In addition to a unique set of designations, the specific plan area is an ideal site for a
form-based code approach to regulate development. Form-based code includes land
development standards that replace traditional use-based zoning codes by using physical
form rather than separation of uses as the organizing principle. Form-based code intends
to produce predictable development results and a high-quality public realm because the
physical form of future development is specifically dictated by the development standards.
Form-based codes focus less on the type of activity taking place inside a building (i.e. the
use) and more on the overall form and character of neighborhoods. While use is still
regulated, more emphasis is placed on the location and form of buildings, the character
of the street frontage, and the relationship between buildings and public spaces (FIGURE
5).

In general, some of the more notable differences between the Palmdale Municipal Code
(PMC) and SPL 20-001, are reduced building setbacks, increased building height,
reduced common and private open space and reduced parking.
Setbacks
PMC Section 17.82.010 requires minimum building setbacks, regardless of development
type as follows:
    Thirty feet, which must include a minimum of 20 feet of landscaping, along arterial
  streets, such as Avenue Q, Palmdale Boulevard, Division Street, etc.; and,
    Twenty feet, which must include 10 feet of landscaping, along local and collector
  streets, such as 3rd Street East, 6th Street East and Avenue P-12.
In addition, PMC Section 17.41.090 requires the following for all single-family residences:
    Minimum front setback of 15 feet;
    Minimum rear setback of 20 feet; and,
    Minimum side setbacks of 10 feet on the side yard adjacent to the garage and five
  feet on the side yard not adjacent to the garage.
Typically, commercial and industrial uses do not require side or rear setbacks, unless the
development is adjacent to residential development, in which case the minimum setback
would be 20 feet.
As proposed, the specific plan requires setbacks for developments within the Urban Core,
Urban Center, General Urban, Regional Commercial and Business Mix designations as
follows:
    Front: five to 15 feet;
    Side: zero to 15 feet; and,
    Rear: zero to 15 feet.
The intent of reducing setbacks is to promote walkability, activate the street by enhancing
visibility and increasing buildable area. While the specific plan also proposes to alter the

Currently, for the zoning designations specified within the specific plan area, the height

PMC Sections 17.42.090 and 17.43.090 require the following:

PMC Section 17.44.090 requires the following:

The PMC does not require common or private open space for designations other than
residential. SPL 20-001 requires common and private open space for residential
development and common open space for commercial development. As specified within

    50 to 100 square feet of private open space for ground floor units;

Development Incentives
SPL 20-001 defines a vision realized over a 30-year period through phased development.
As the City awaits arrival of high-speed rail, the PTASP provides both requirements and
offers interim incentives to attract developers to aid development in certain locations and
at certain densities. The PTASP establishes minimum densities in three zoning districts
to ensure that the properties, especially those that are currently vacant or under-utilized,
develop at desired densities that leverage the presence of anticipated transit
opportunities.
The PTASP also proposes making public space improvements in the areas around the
future multi-modal high-speed rail station to enhance the community and create
